explanations.answer: Set them free from the law of sin and death
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Romans 8:2 says it plainly: “…the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death.” Free means free. That's an unlocked door, not a bigger ring of keys.

explanations.answer: Made them strong enough to obey every rule
explanations.explanation: I see why that sounds right, because strength feels like the fix for everything. But the verse never says that. It says the law of the Spirit of life “set you free from the law of sin and death.” The word is free, and I'm not adding a word the verse doesn't use.

explanations.answer: Gave them a list of new rules to keep
explanations.explanation: A new list is a natural guess, friend. Romans 8:2 doesn't hand over a list, though. It says the law of the Spirit of life “set you free from the law of sin and death.” That's a rescue, not a reading assignment.

explanations.answer: He sent His own Son as an offering for sin
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Romans 8:3 says God did it “by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin.” The law couldn't do it, so God Himself did. It's the whole letter in one verse, and I'm just standing here with my mustache in the air.

explanations.answer: He gave His people a stricter law to follow
explanations.explanation: A stricter law, huh? That's the opposite direction, friend. The verse says the law was already powerless to do this, so more law isn't the answer. What God did was send “His own Son” as “an offering for sin” (Romans 8:3).

explanations.answer: He sent His prophets with one more warning
explanations.explanation: One more warning is a fair guess, since warnings are a thing in the Bible. But that isn't what this verse says. Romans 8:3 says God sent “His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin.” The Son, not another messenger, is the answer here.

True, baker. Romans 8:3 says God sent His Son “as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the flesh.” Look where the condemning lands: on sin. Verse 1 already told us there's no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.

Careful, friend, this one is true. Romans 8:3 says God sent His own Son “as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the flesh.” So the text says exactly what the question says. And the condemning lands on sin, not on those in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

explanations.answer: So the law's righteous standard is fulfilled in us
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Romans 8:4 says it was “so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us.” Fulfilled, not thrown out. God had a purpose, and it was good.

explanations.answer: So the law could be set aside for good
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, but Romans 8:4 goes another way. The verse says it was “so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us.” Fulfilled is a long way from set aside. The text keeps the law's standard and says it gets met.

explanations.answer: So people would try harder to keep the law
explanations.explanation: Trying harder is the classic move, friend. I've tried harder at plenty of things and the dough still did what it wanted. Romans 8:4 gives a different purpose: “so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us.” It doesn't say a word about trying harder.

That's it, baker. Romans 8:6 says, “The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” Life AND peace. That's a two-for-one, and I didn't even have to put a coupon in the box.

Wisdom is a good word, and the Bible loves it. But it isn't the word in this verse. Romans 8:6 says the mind of the Spirit is “life and peace.” Death and life sit on opposite sides there, and wisdom isn't on the scale.

Power sounds like a strong pick, friend. Romans 8:6 uses a different word, though. It says, “…the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” Life is set right across from death, which is why that word is the one that fits.

explanations.answer: Because it is hostile to God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Romans 8:7 gives the reason: “…because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God.” It goes on to say that it “does not submit to God's law, nor can it do so.” Hostile is a strong word, and the verse chose it.

explanations.answer: Because it is too weak to try
explanations.explanation: Too weak sounds gentle, and that's the problem, because the verse is not gentle here. Romans 8:7 says the mind of the flesh is death “because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God.” The reason given is hostility, not weakness.

explanations.answer: Because it never hears God's law
explanations.explanation: Hearing the law is a fair thing to wonder about, friend. But Romans 8:7 doesn't say the flesh never hears it. It says the mind of the flesh is “hostile to God” and “does not submit to God's law.” Not submitting is a different thing from not hearing.

Not quite, friend, because the text says the reverse. Romans 8:8 says, “Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God.” The question's own first sentence points the same way: the mind of the flesh “does not submit to God's law, nor can it do so.” So that makes this one False.

False is right, baker. Romans 8:8 says, “Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God.” The word is cannot, and it's one the verse doesn't soften. And right after it comes the good news for those with the Spirit (Romans 8:9).
You've got it, baker. Romans 8:9 says, “And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.” Belong is the word. It's about whose you are, not just what you do.
Listening matters, but it isn't the word here. Romans 8:9 says, “…if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.” It's about belonging, friend, not about listening.

Praying is a good thing, and the Bible has plenty of it. This verse uses a different word, though. Romans 8:9 says anyone without the Spirit of Christ “does not belong to Christ.” The word it lands on is belong.

True, baker, and it's a big one. Romans 8:11 says, “…He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you.” Same Spirit, same power at work in us. I'd shout, but my mustache is already waving.

This one is True, friend. Romans 8:11 says, “…if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you.” So it's exactly what the question says. It's great news, and I'm glad you got to read it again.
That's right, baker. Romans 8:13 says, “…if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Die on one side, live on the other. The verse doesn't leave much room in the middle.

Rest sounds lovely, friend, and I'm all for a nap after a long batch. But Romans 8:13 doesn't use that word. It says, “…if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Set right against die, the word is live.

Stumbling is something I know about, since I once tripped over a rolling pin. But that isn't the word in this verse. Romans 8:13 sets “you will die” against “you will live.” The ending it gives for the Spirit is life.

explanations.answer: The Spirit of adoption to sonship
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Romans 8:15 says, “…you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” Not a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but the Spirit of adoption. The verse puts the two side by side.

explanations.answer: A spirit of service under the law
explanations.explanation: That one's close to the slave side of the verse, and I can see why it caught your eye. But Romans 8:15 doesn't name it as what they received. It says, “you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship.” Adoption is the answer.

explanations.answer: A spirit of courage for the battle
explanations.explanation: Courage is a fine thing to wish for, friend. This verse isn't talking about a battle, though. Romans 8:15 says what they received was “the Spirit of adoption to sonship.” That's the one the text names.

Right, baker. Romans 8:16 says, “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children.” The Spirit speaks with our spirit. I'd say that's about as good a witness as you can ask for.

The law is all over this passage, so I see why you'd reach for it. But Romans 8:16 doesn't give the law this job. It says, “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children.” The one who testifies is the Spirit.

A conscience is a reasonable guess, friend. Romans 8:16 doesn't name it, though. It says, “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children.” So the one speaking up is the Spirit, and He does it with our spirit.
You got it, baker. Romans 8:17 says, “And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.” Children means heirs. The verse goes right from one to the other.

Messengers carry a message, and that's an honest job. But it's not what this verse says. Romans 8:17 says, “And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.” The word it gives is heirs, friend.

Priests is a good word and it shows up elsewhere in Scripture. But in Romans 8:17 the text says, “And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.” So the answer here is heirs.

That's right, baker. Romans 8:17 says, “…if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.” It's a heavy word, and I'll say that plainly. The verse puts suffering with Him and being glorified with Him together.

Rest would be an easier word to land on, friend, and I wish it were the one. But Romans 8:17 says, “…if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.” The verse names suffering, so that's the answer.

Working with Him sounds like something a bakery would love, I'll admit. But this verse doesn't say work. Romans 8:17 says, “…if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.” The word it uses is suffer.
